text.p: Shares in Anglo-Dutch consumer products group Unilever NV /Plc rose further on Monday after last week's gains as enthusiasm for its strategy to sell chemical businesses continued, analysts said.
"There is talk that quite a few companies are interested so the market is hoping Unilever will get a top-notch price," said one analyst who asked not to be named.

Last week, when it reported a 15 percent gain in year pretax profits to 2.66 billion pounds ($4.3 billion), Unilever said it would sell its four speciality chemicals units, National Starch and Chemical Company, Quest International, Unichema International and Crosfield.
Analysts said the businesses, which might be sold separately or be picked up together, could raise between four and six billion pounds.
Several potential buyers have been suggested by analysts, including Germany's Hoechst, Degussa and Henkel.

Unilever co-chairman Niall FitzGerald told the Sunday Telegraph newspaper that "there is a great deal of interest and offers are being prepared as it is the last major chance to realign the chemical industry."
"All the businesses up for sale are quality groups, they are the number one or two in their field," the analyst said.
FitzGerald has said he would hope to conclude a sale in the next three to six months.
On Monday Unilever shares trading in London ended up 64-1/2 pence to 16.02 pounds, while in Amsterdam they rose 16.20 guilders to 367.20.
Analysts said the market was also looking ahead to what use Unilever might make of the proceeds from the sale.

FitzGerald said last week that funds would be used for acquisitions in growth areas, such as Asia Pacific and South America, and in priority categories like detergents, tea, ice cream, yellow fats, personal care products and fragrances.
"I would like to see a combination of acquisitions and organic growth," one sector analyst said.
Another said he would be looking for "a significant amount" to be put into investment, particularly for organic growth in emerging markets.
"I would not want it all spent on acquisitions, there could be lots of growth in emerging markets and building in established ones," the analyst said.
Analysts said several possible acquisitions had been rumoured for Unilever, including food group Heinz and the Campbell's Soups business of Reckitt & Coleman.
But they added that any such purchase was likely to be friendly as Unilever is considered averse to hostile takeovers, while one analyst questioned the added value of buying such brands.
"You have to ask what these buys would bring to emerging markets, that's where the focus seems to be," the analyst said.
"But if there is no significant acquisition in two years, a special dividend could be on the cards," he added.
Analysts said sale of the chemicals businesses would also help Unilever to focus on its core activities, which could also strengthen its prospects.
"Selling the chemicals units provides the opportunity to focus down on its core strengths," the analyst said.
But analysts added that FitzGerald, who stepped into the co-chairman's role in September 1996, was the driving force behind the attempts to change Unilever's previously sluggish image.
"FitzGerald is the catalyst. Unilever could have bought things in the past. With him on board, the market is backing him to make more good decisions," the analyst said. ($ = 0.617 British Pounds)
